summary: This is a clipped en-academic.com (Wikipedia-derived) dictionary entry for the Intermontane Belt, a physiographic region in British Columbia, Canada. The article describes its rolling hills, high plateaus and deeply cut valleys, and explains that its granitic rocks relate to volcanic activity of an ancient island arc and to the later buildup of Insular Belt rocks. It notes that the island arc which collided with North America to form the belt is called the Intermontane Islands. The page also lists related dictionary entries such as Intermontane Plate, Intermontane Islands, Insular Belt and Omineca Arc; the surrounding navigation, ads and scripts are boilerplate.
one_line: Wikipedia-derived entry describing the Intermontane Belt, a physiographic region of British Columbia, Canada, and its island-arc geology.
key_facts: The Intermontane Belt is a physiographic region in British Columbia, Canada.
The Intermontane Belt has rolling hills, high plateaus and deeply cut valleys.
The rocks in the Intermontane Belt have very little similarities with North America.
Granitic rocks in the region are related to the volcanic activity of an ancient island arc.
The granitic rocks are also related to the later buildup of Insular Belt rocks.
The island arc that collided against North America to form the belt is called the Intermontane Islands.
The Intermontane Plate was an ancient oceanic tectonic plate that lay on the west coast of North America about 195 million years ago.
The Intermontane Islands were a giant chain of active volcanic islands in the Pacific Ocean during the Triassic time beginning around 245 million years ago.
The Insular Belt is a physio geological region on the north western North American coast consisting of three major island groups and many smaller islands.
The Insular Belt stretches from Southern British Columbia into Alaska and the Yukon.
The Omineca Arc or Omineca Belt was a Jurassic through Cretaceous volcanic arc terrane in western North America, extending from Alaska through Yukon and British Columbia to Washington.
The article's source attribution is Wikimedia Foundation, 2010.
The related external link is titled Physiography of British Columbia.
